weak.text:
Cellphones should not be used all the time in class. Sometimes they can help but sometimes they make problems. I think the teacher should say when we can use them because the teacher knows the lesson. If everybody uses a phone whenever they like, people will talk to friends and not listen.

A phone can help to find a word in a dictionary. This is useful if we are reading and do not understand a word. But not everybody has data or a good phone, so the teacher should give a book or paper too. It is not fair if one learner can finish because they have a phone and another learner cannot.

Phones can make a noise when a message comes. This can stop the class from listening. A learner might also take a photo of someone without asking. The teacher should make rules about phones and privacy. If phones are not needed, they should be in a bag.

Some learners say phones are important for emergencies. If something happens, the school office can help the learner contact their family. Learners can speak to the teacher if there is a real emergency. This means the class can still have a rule while people get help when they need it.

In conclusion, phones should only be used when the teacher says they are useful for a lesson. Everyone should get another option if they do not have a phone. This can help learners focus and make the rule fair. Every learner should have a chance to participate.

middle.text:
Cellphones are common in South African schools, but learners and teachers do not always agree about using them in class. I think they should be allowed for planned activities only. A complete ban may remove a useful tool, while unrestricted use can distract the class. Teachers should decide when a phone supports the lesson.

For example, learners can use a dictionary app to check the meaning of a word. They could also complete a short quiz chosen by the teacher. These activities can save time, but the phone should not replace careful reading or discussion. Learners should explain what they learned instead of simply copying information from a screen.

There must be another option for learners who do not have a device or data. A printed worksheet or shared school tablet can make the activity more equal. If only learners with personal phones can take part, the policy is not fair. Schools should also explain the rules to families so that everyone understands them.

Phones can interrupt learning when messages arrive. Cameras can also cause privacy problems if a learner takes a photo without permission. Teachers can ask learners to keep phones silent and put them away when they are not needed. A consistent rule across classes would help learners know what to expect.

Some people believe phones should never be allowed because they cause distraction. This is a serious concern, but teaching responsible use can also prepare learners for work and further study. The school should set limits and apply them fairly.

In conclusion, phones should be allowed only for a clear learning purpose and with teacher permission. This approach supports useful activities while protecting attention and privacy. Schools should review the rule with learners and families when it is not working.

strong.text:
Schools should allow cellphones in classrooms only when a teacher has chosen a purposeful activity. A total ban ignores the ways a phone can support learning, but unrestricted access treats every moment as suitable for screen use. A clear, teacher-led policy can protect attention while helping learners practise responsible technology use.

Consider a Grade 10 learner who meets an unfamiliar word while reading an English passage. A dictionary app can give a quick definition, after which the learner can explain the word in context. A teacher-selected quiz can also show which ideas need another explanation. In both cases the phone serves a specific learning goal; it does not replace the teacher's feedback or the learner's own reasoning.

However, a phone policy must not make access to learning depend on family income. Some learners have no device, limited data or an unreliable connection. A school should offer printed materials or a shared device before an activity begins. That alternative is not an optional kindness: it is necessary for a fair classroom where every learner can complete the same task.

Distraction and privacy are genuine risks. A notification can interrupt a difficult explanation, and taking a photograph without permission can harm another learner. Phones should remain silent and out of sight unless the teacher has invited their use. The school should explain consequences in advance and apply them consistently, rather than expecting each teacher to invent a different rule.

Supporters of a complete ban may argue that it is easier to enforce. Simplicity matters, especially when a class is large, but a carefully limited rule is still clear: teacher permission is required, and phones are away at other times. Learners gain practice in making responsible choices without being given unlimited access.

Therefore, cellphones should be permitted for planned learning activities, with non-digital alternatives and firm privacy rules. This balanced policy keeps the lesson in control of the teacher, includes learners with different resources and teaches a practical skill for life beyond school.
